data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive methodological rule of 'risk minimization' rather than a probabilistic prediction; however, accepting this defense costs the agent any rational assurance that the future will resemble the past, reducing scientific action to a gamble where the 'best' choice is merely the one with the most exposed and surviving falsification attempts, not the one most likely to succeed.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference for the better-corroborated theory implicitly assumes that past test results are relevant to future performance, it smuggles in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's concept of 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) cannot be formally defined without collapsing into probabilistic terms, the non-inductive basis fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory necessarily implies a belief in its future reliability, then the distinction between 'methodological rule' and 'inductive belief' is merely semantic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction/probability) and 'criticism' (which relies on logical consistency and severity of tests). Preference is framed not as an expectation of truth or success, but as the selection of the theory that has withstood the most severe attempts at falsification, thereby offering the highest informational content and the clearest potential for future error detection. This avoids induction by refusing to claim the future will mirror the past, instead claiming only that the chosen theory is currently the least refuted.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
